migrationNotes: Spine: two trolley cases with the same arithmetic are compared until the difference is found in what the plan needs from the victim, and that difference is followed through Kant's two formulas, his two kinds of command and the older rule of double effect.

lesson.title: Duty, persons and the footbridge

steps.headline: What the plan needs from the victim

lead.text: To find what separates the two cases, look at each plan as a piece of machinery. In Case A the plan is to turn the trolley away from the five. It happens that the side track has one person on it, and he is killed. But suppose the side track were empty. The plan would still work and the trolley would still be turned. The death of the one is a foreseen result of the plan, and the plan does not rely on it.
Case B is different. The plan is to stop the trolley with the stranger's body. Take the stranger away and nothing stops the trolley, so the plan fails. His body is a working part of the plan.

afterFigure.text: Philosophers have names for these two roles. When a harm to someone is how your plan works, you are using that person as a means. When a harm is a result that the plan merely brings along, and the plan would work just as well without it, the harm is a side effect. The distinction has nothing to do with how many people die.

lead.text: Apply the test from the last screen to both cases: would the plan still work if the one person were not there?
Now do the sum a utilitarian would do for the footbridge, setting the distinction between means and side effect aside.

reveal.text: The count matches the switch: four more people survive. A theory that only counts outcomes cannot tell the two cases apart.

lead.text: Kant would not be surprised that the count fails to settle the matter. For him, morality starts from what we owe to persons, who can set goals of their own and decide how to live. He called that ability humanity, using the word in his own sense: the rational nature that every person shares.

One of his tests follows from it. Always treat persons as ends in themselves, and never merely as a means. To treat someone as an end is to respect that they have purposes of their own, so you cannot simply override them. Using a person as a tool, as a working part of your plan and without their agreement, fails to show that respect. Kant called this the formula of humanity.

The word 'merely' matters. Using people as means is part of ordinary life, as when you use the baker to get your bread. What the formula forbids is treating someone only as a means, as though their own purposes counted for nothing. The stranger on the footbridge has not agreed to be a brake for the trolley.

steps.headline: Apply the idea of a means to the footbridge push.

workedSteps.text: State the plan: the stranger's body will stop the trolley.
Ask whether the plan works without him. It fails, so his death is how it works.
A plan that needs a person's body treats him as a tool. That is what the formula of humanity forbids.

steps.headline: Name Kant's formulation about how to treat persons.

workedSteps.text: Kant says to treat people always as ends, and never merely as a means.
This is called the formula of ___.

lead.text: Kant gave a second test, and it looks at the rule behind an act and not at who is affected. A maxim is the rule you are acting on, put as 'in this situation I will do this, for this reason'. The test asks whether you could will that everyone act on your maxim. If the maxim only works because most other people do not follow it, you cannot consistently will it for everyone.

Take the maxim of someone who needs money: 'I will promise to repay a loan, knowing I cannot, to get the cash.' Suppose everybody acted on it. Then nobody would believe a promise to repay, since everyone would know that promises are made to be broken. But then no one would lend, and the maxim could not be acted on. It defeats itself. Compare 'I will repay what I borrow', which still works when everyone follows it.

afterFigure.text: This test is called the formula of universal law: act only on a maxim that you can at the same time will to become a universal law. The objection to the false promise is not that universal lying would have bad results. It is that the maxim cannot be consistently universalised, because it depends on a practice, promising, that it would destroy.

premises.text: My maxim: when I need money, I will promise to repay it, knowing I cannot.
If everyone acted on this maxim, no one would believe a promise to repay.
If no one believed such promises, the maxim could not be acted on.

conclusion.text: I cannot will the maxim as a universal law, so the false promise is forbidden.

premises.text: My maxim: when I borrow money, I will repay it as promised.
If everyone acted on this maxim, promises to repay would remain credible.

conclusion.text: I can will this maxim as a universal law.

lead.text: A maxim can be tested the same way whatever its subject. Try one about queues.

reveal.text: That is the formula of universal law: could the maxim hold for everyone? Universalised, this one destroys the queue it relies on.

lead.text: Kant noticed that commands differ in how far they depend on what you happen to want. 'If you want to pass the exam, revise' speaks only to people who have that goal. Someone who does not care about the exam can ignore it. Kant called commands of this kind hypothetical imperatives, since they hold only on a condition.

He thought morality does not work that way. 'Do not use people merely as means' does not say 'if you want to be moral'. It binds you whatever you want, and Kant called a command like that a categorical imperative. The formula of humanity and the formula of universal law are two ways of stating the one categorical imperative of morality.

A categorical command has a different standing from prudent advice. It tells you what to do even when doing it costs you something you wanted. That is why Kant treats keeping a promise as a duty and not only as a sensible policy for being trusted.

steps.headline: Foreseeing a harm and intending it

lead.text: Case A and Case B can now be separated more carefully. In Case A the death of the one is a side effect of turning the trolley. In Case B it is the means. Medieval thinkers worked out a rule built on this same difference, and it is traced to Thomas Aquinas, who discussed killing in self-defence. It is called the doctrine of double effect.

The doctrine says that an act with two effects, one good and one bad, may be allowed when the good effect is what you aim at and the bad one is only foreseen. The bad effect must not be your means to the good one, and the good must outweigh the bad. The standard example is a doctor who gives a dying patient enough painkiller to ease her pain, knowing that it may shorten her life. The lever fits the rule. The footbridge does not, since the stranger's death is the means.
The doctrine gives one of the clearest accounts of why the two cases feel different, though not everyone is satisfied with it.
Apply what you have just read about foreseen effects to a new case, away from trolleys.

reveal.text: The doctrine of double effect: a foreseen side effect may be permitted, while harm intended as a means may not.

lesson.orientation: Apply Kant's universal-law and humanity formulations, and compare the switch and footbridge cases.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A runaway trolley is heading for five people on the main track. In Case A, which you met in the last lesson, you pull a lever and the trolley turns onto a side track, where it kills one person instead. Nearly everyone says that you may pull it.

Case B changes the setting. You are standing on a footbridge above the track, next to a heavy stranger. The only way to stop the trolley is to push him off, so that his body blocks it. One person dies and five live, exactly as in Case A. Yet most people feel at once that pushing him is wrong, even people who would pull the lever without a second thought.

Counting lives cannot explain the difference, since the count is the same. Something else about the two cases must matter. In this lesson you find out what it is, using ideas from the German philosopher Immanuel Kant, and you test them on promises and on a rule that medieval thinkers worked out long before him.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell harm used as a means from harm as a side effect, and apply two of Kant's tests.

recap.keyIdea: Kant's tests ask how we treat people, not only how many we save. Using a person as a means is forbidden, and a maxim that cannot be universalised is ruled out.

blocks.text: You counted four lives saved in the footbridge case and asked whether the plan needed the stranger's body. You then tested a false promise and a queue by imagining everyone acting on the same maxim.

recap.nextHook: Kant asks which rules an act must respect. The next lesson turns to a different question, what kind of person to be, and begins with a coach working out how much training a beginner and a champion should each do.

questions.prompt: From a footbridge you could push a heavy stranger onto the track; his body would stop a trolley that will otherwise kill five. Counting lives only, how many more people survive if you push?
hints: Count deaths if you do nothing.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Not pushing: five die. Pushing: the stranger dies. 5 − 1 = 4, the same as the switch case.

questions.onCorrect: Four more survive: five die if you do nothing, one if you push. The count matches the switch.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the deaths if you do nothing. Subtract the death if you push.
That adds the deaths. You are comparing two options, not totalling them.

questions.prompt: Kant's formulation that you must never treat a person merely as a means is called the formula of ___. Fill the gap with one word.
hints: Kant says we must treat it, in ourselves and others, always as an end.
The word names what all persons share, in Kant's sense of rational nature.
questions.onCorrect: The formula of humanity: persons are always to be treated as ends.

misconceptions.feedback: That is another formulation. The one about persons is named after what all persons share.

questions.prompt: Kant tests the maxim 'I will push to the front of a queue whenever I am in a hurry' by asking whether everyone could act on it. If everyone did, queues would collapse and the maxim would have nothing to work against. Which of Kant's formulas is this test?
hints: The test imagines the maxim adopted by everyone.
Its name says the maxim must be able to become a law for all.
questions.onCorrect: The formula of universal law: could the maxim hold for everyone?

misconceptions.feedback: That formulation concerns how to treat persons. This test imagines the maxim adopted by everyone.

questions.prompt: A fire crew lights a controlled burn to save a village, knowing it will destroy one farmer's barn, which they would spare if they could. Name the doctrine, traced to Aquinas, that may permit a foreseen harm like this as a side effect of a good act but forbids intending harm as a means.
hints: One act has two effects: one the crew aims at and one they merely foresee.
questions.onCorrect: The doctrine of double effect: a foreseen side effect may be permitted, an intended means may not.

misconceptions.feedback: That is part of the doctrine. Its name counts the effects of one act.

questions.prompt: 'If you want to be trusted, keep your promises.' What kind of imperative is this, in Kant's terms?
hints: Does the command depend on a goal you happen to have?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It binds only someone who has the stated goal of being trusted, so it is hypothetical. A categorical imperative binds whatever you want.

questions.onCorrect: Hypothetical: it binds only someone who wants to be trusted. A categorical imperative binds whatever you want.

misconceptions.feedback: A categorical imperative binds whatever you want. This one depends on a goal.
Universal names a formulation, not a kind of imperative.

questions.prompt: In Thomson's loop case the side track rejoins the main line, so only the one person's body stops the trolley. Is that person's death a means or a side effect of saving the five?
hints: Ask whether the plan would still work if the one person were absent.
If the plan needs his body, his death is part of how it works.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A means: if the one were not on the loop, the trolley would come round and kill the five.

questions.onCorrect: A means: if the one were absent, the trolley would come round and kill the five.

misconceptions.feedback: Ask whether the plan would still work if he were absent. If it needs his body, his death is part of how it works.

questions.prompt: Case A: you pull a lever and a trolley that would kill five people kills one person on a side track instead. Case B: you push a heavy stranger off a footbridge, and his body stops the trolley. In which case is a person's body the way you save the five? Answer A or B.
hints: Ask in which case the plan would fail if the one person were not there.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Case B: the stranger's body is what stops the trolley.

questions.onCorrect: In Case B the plan needs the stranger's body. In Case A the one is hit only because the trolley goes that way.

misconceptions.feedback: In Case A the trolley is turned away. Ask in which case the plan would fail if the one person were absent.

questions.prompt: Maxim: “I will keep a promise only when it suits me.” If everyone acted on it, could promising still work as a practice? Answer yes or no.
